questions.q: What are the default values of fields and local variables?
questions.a: Fields get type defaults: 0 for numeric types, false for boolean, null for references. Local variables get no default and must be initialised before use.
questions.explain: The compiler rejects reading an uninitialised local. Fields are zeroed when the object is allocated, which is why null fields surprise people later.
questions.example: int field; // 0 inside a class; int local; // compile error if read
questions.followUp: Why does Java not default-initialise locals?
questions.tip: Contrast fields and locals explicitly — that is the point of the question.
questions.code: class Box { int value; } // new Box().value == 0

questions.q: if/else vs switch: when do you choose which?
questions.a: Use if for ranges and complex boolean conditions; use switch for a fixed set of discrete values. A switch expression returns a value and is exhaustive for enums and sealed types.
questions.explain: Arrow cases avoid accidental fall-through. Modern switch also supports patterns, guards and null handling.
questions.example: String size = switch (code) { case 1 -> "small"; default -> "other"; };
questions.followUp: What is fall-through and how do you avoid it?
questions.tip: Mention switch expressions, not just the classic statement.

questions.q: for vs while vs do-while?
questions.a: for when the iteration count is known and the counter is local to the loop; while when the condition drives repetition; do-while when the body must run at least once.
questions.explain: The enhanced for iterates arrays and Iterables without index bookkeeping and cannot easily remove elements.
questions.example: for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) is the standard counted loop.
questions.followUp: When is a do-while a genuinely better choice?
questions.tip: Give a real do-while case such as a menu that must render once.
questions.code:
int i = 0;
while (i < 3) { System.out.println(i); i++; }

questions.q: break vs continue vs return?
questions.a: break exits the nearest loop or switch; continue skips to the next iteration; return leaves the whole method.
questions.explain: In nested loops break only exits the inner loop. Use a labelled break or extract a method with return to exit both.
questions.example: for (...) { if (skip) continue; if (done) break; }
questions.followUp: How do you break out of two nested loops cleanly?
questions.tip: Mention labelled break but recommend extracting a method.

questions.q: What does a method signature include?
questions.a: Name plus parameter types (and order). Return type and parameter names are not part of the signature, so you cannot overload on return type alone.
questions.explain: The compiler resolves overloads using the static types of the arguments, including widening, boxing and varargs in a defined order.
questions.example: sum(int, int) and sum(long, long) are different signatures.
questions.followUp: Can two methods differ only by throws clause?
questions.tip: Say clearly that return type is not part of the signature.
questions.code:
static int sum(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
static long sum(long a, long b) { return a + b; }

questions.q: Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?
questions.a: Always pass-by-value: the value of the variable is copied. For objects, the copied value is the reference, so the callee can mutate the object but cannot reassign the caller's variable.
questions.explain: Reassigning the parameter inside the method has no effect outside. Mutating the referenced object is visible to the caller.
questions.example: void add(List<String> l) { l.add("x"); } changes the caller's list.
questions.followUp: How do you make an object argument effectively immutable?
questions.tip: Say 'pass-by-value of the reference' — that is the precise answer.
questions.code:
static void replace(List<String> list) { list = new ArrayList<>(); }
// caller's list is unchanged

questions.q: Which String methods should you know cold?
questions.a: length, charAt, substring(begin,end), indexOf, contains, startsWith, endsWith, split, replace, trim/strip, toUpperCase, equals, compareTo, and formatted.
questions.explain: substring's end is exclusive, split takes a regex, and trim removes only ASCII whitespace while strip handles Unicode.
questions.example: "java".substring(1, 3) returns "av".
questions.followUp: How do you check for a blank string?
questions.tip: Mention isBlank() for whitespace-only strings.
questions.code:
String s = "  java  ";
System.out.println(s.strip()); // java

questions.q: How do you copy and compare arrays?
questions.a: Copy with Arrays.copyOf, clone or System.arraycopy; compare content with Arrays.equals (deepEquals for nested arrays). == compares references.
questions.explain: Arrays.toString gives readable output for logs and failing tests. Sorting uses Arrays.sort, or parallelSort for large arrays.
questions.example: Arrays.equals(new int[]{1}, new int[]{1}) is true.
questions.followUp: Does clone() deep-copy an object array?
questions.tip: Note that clone is shallow for object elements.

questions.q: What is null and what is NullPointerException?
questions.a: null means a reference points to no object. Dereferencing it (field access, method call, unboxing, array access) throws NullPointerException.
questions.explain: Defensive checks, Optional for return values, and Objects.requireNonNull at boundaries reduce NPEs. Annotations such as @Nullable help tooling.
questions.example: String s = null; s.length() throws NPE.
questions.followUp: What does Optional actually solve?
questions.tip: Say Optional is for return types, not fields.
questions.code:
String s = null;
System.out.println(s == null ? "missing" : s.length());

questions.q: What are packages and imports for?
questions.a: Packages namespace classes and control access; imports bring simple names into scope. java.lang is imported automatically.
questions.explain: The package must match the directory layout for build tools. A fully qualified name avoids ambiguity when two packages contain the same class.
questions.example: import java.util.List; then write List<String>.
questions.followUp: What is the default package and why avoid it?
questions.tip: Mention that imports do not load classes, they only resolve names.
questions.code:
package com.brocode.app;

import java.util.List;

questions.q: Compile-time error vs runtime exception vs error?
questions.a: Compile-time errors stop javac (syntax, type mismatch). Runtime exceptions are thrown during execution. Errors (such as OutOfMemoryError) signal serious JVM problems that applications usually should not catch.
questions.explain: A program that compiles can still fail logically; tests and assertions catch that class of bug.
questions.example: Missing semicolon: compile error. Array index out of bounds: runtime exception.
questions.followUp: Should you catch Throwable?
questions.tip: Do not catch Error in normal application code.

questions.q: Why write Javadoc and how is it different from comments?
questions.a: Javadoc is structured documentation attached to public API and rendered by the javadoc tool. Ordinary comments explain implementation and are not extracted.
questions.explain: Write Javadoc for contracts: what a method does, parameters, return value and thrown exceptions — not for restating the code.
questions.example: /** Returns the sum. @param a first addend @return a + b */
questions.followUp: What Javadoc tags matter most?
questions.tip: Say that outdated Javadoc is worse than none.
questions.code:
/**
 * Adds two numbers.
 * @param a first addend
 * @param b second addend
 * @return the sum
 */
static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }

questions.q: Stack vs heap in Java?
questions.a: Each thread has a stack of frames holding locals, parameters and partial results; objects and arrays live on the shared heap. References live on the stack (or inside other heap objects).
questions.explain: Stack memory is reclaimed automatically when a method returns; heap memory is reclaimed by the garbage collector. Deep recursion overflows the stack.
questions.example: A local int is on the stack; new int[1000] allocates on the heap.
questions.followUp: Why does recursion cause StackOverflowError?
questions.tip: Say objects are on the heap but references can be anywhere.

questions.q: Explain the order of initialisation when an object is created.
questions.a: Static initialisers and static fields run once when the class is first used; then instance field initialisers and instance initialiser blocks run in textual order, then the constructor body.
questions.explain: The superclass constructor runs before the subclass's fields are initialised, so calling an overridable method from a constructor can observe uninitialised subclass state.
questions.example: A constructor calling a method that reads a not-yet-assigned subclass field sees 0 or null.
questions.followUp: Why should constructors avoid calling overridable methods?
questions.tip: Mention the superclass-first rule and the overridable-method trap.

questions.q: What are exception best practices?
questions.a: Catch only what you can handle, catch specific types, never swallow silently, wrap with context and preserve the cause, and do not use exceptions for normal control flow.
questions.explain: Logging and rethrowing causes duplicate noise; pick one boundary that logs. Clean up with try-with-resources rather than finally.
questions.example: throw new IllegalStateException("account " + id + " is closed", e);
questions.followUp: What does it mean to preserve the cause?
questions.tip: Mention the cause chain in the constructor.

questions.q: How does finally interact with return and exceptions?
questions.a: finally always runs (except on System.exit or JVM crash). A return in finally overrides a pending return and discards exceptions, which is why returning from finally is banned in most style guides.
questions.explain: An exception thrown in finally replaces the original one; try-with-resources instead suppresses close failures onto the primary exception.
questions.example: try { return 5; } finally { return 0; } returns 0.
questions.followUp: When is finally still necessary?
questions.tip: Say 'never return from finally' as a rule.

questions.q: List.of vs Arrays.asList vs Collections.unmodifiableList?
questions.a: List.of is immutable, rejects nulls, and is a compact value-based list. Arrays.asList is a fixed-size view backed by the array (set allowed, add/remove not). unmodifiableList is a read-only view over a mutable list.
questions.explain: A view still reflects changes to the backing collection; List.of is truly independent and immutable.
questions.example: Arrays.asList(1,2).add(3) throws UnsupportedOperationException.
questions.followUp: How do you get a mutable copy?
questions.tip: new ArrayList<>(List.of(...)) is the usual mutable copy.

questions.q: entrySet vs keySet vs values?
questions.a: keySet iterates keys, values iterates values, entrySet iterates key-value pairs and is the efficient choice when you need both.
questions.explain: Iterating keySet and calling get(key) for each entry does a second lookup per element and can be wrong if the map changes.
questions.example: for (Map.Entry<K,V> e : map.entrySet()) use both e.getKey() and e.getValue().
questions.followUp: Can you remove entries through entrySet?
questions.tip: Mention entrySet().removeIf for filtering.
questions.code:
for (Map.Entry<String, Integer> e : map.entrySet())
    System.out.println(e.getKey() + "=" + e.getValue());

questions.q: How does a HashSet work?
questions.a: It is backed by a HashMap where elements are keys and a shared placeholder is the value. add computes hashCode, finds the bucket, then checks equals.
questions.explain: Duplicate detection depends on both methods. Mutable elements are dangerous because their hash can change after insertion.
questions.example: Adding the same String twice keeps one element and returns false the second time.
questions.followUp: What is the average complexity of contains?
questions.tip: Say 'HashSet is a HashMap with dummy values'.

questions.q: HashMap vs TreeMap vs LinkedHashMap?
questions.a: HashMap is unordered and fastest on average; TreeMap keeps keys sorted with O(log n) operations and needs Comparable or a Comparator; LinkedHashMap keeps insertion or access order.
questions.explain: LinkedHashMap with accessOrder=true is the basis of a simple LRU cache via removeEldestEntry.
questions.example: new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) for LRU.
questions.followUp: How would you build an LRU cache with the standard library?
questions.tip: Give the accessOrder + removeEldestEntry recipe.

questions.q: Deque vs Stack?
questions.a: Stack is a legacy synchronized class; Deque (usually ArrayDeque) is the modern choice for stack and queue behaviour, offering push/pop and addLast/pollFirst.
questions.explain: ArrayDeque is faster and not synchronized, and it rejects nulls. Use java.util.concurrent structures when threads share it.
questions.example: Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>(); stack.push(1);
questions.followUp: Which deque operation is FIFO?
questions.tip: Say 'do not use java.util.Stack in new code'.

questions.q: When should you use var?
questions.a: Use var when the type is obvious from the initialiser and the variable is local. Avoid it when it hides the type, in field declarations (not allowed), or when the inferred type is an implementation detail.
questions.explain: var is compile-time inference, not dynamic typing. The variable still has a fixed static type.
questions.example: var users = new HashMap<String, List<User>>(); is readable; var x = get(); is not.
questions.followUp: Can var be used in a lambda parameter?
questions.tip: Emphasise readability over brevity.
questions.code:
var counts = new HashMap<String, Integer>();
for (var entry : counts.entrySet()) { }

questions.q: What is a switch expression and what rules apply?
questions.a: It returns a value, uses arrow labels, requires exhaustiveness (default or all enum/sealed cases), and every branch must produce a compatible value. yield returns from a block.
questions.explain: Exhaustiveness is checked for enums and sealed hierarchies, so adding a case later becomes a compile error instead of a silent fallthrough bug.
questions.example: int days = switch (month) { case 2 -> 28; case 4, 6, 9, 11 -> 30; default -> 31; };
questions.followUp: How does pattern matching in switch help?
questions.tip: Mention that no fall-through is possible with arrows.

questions.q: What are text blocks and when do you use them?
questions.a: Text blocks are multi-line string literals delimited by three double quotes. They preserve newlines, strip incidental indentation and are ideal for SQL, JSON and HTML.
questions.explain: Use \s to keep a trailing space and \ to join lines without a newline. Formatted fills placeholders.
questions.example: String json = """\n{"id": 1}\n""";
questions.followUp: How does indentation stripping work?
questions.tip: Mention that the closing delimiter position sets the common indentation.
questions.code:
String sql = """
    SELECT id, name
    FROM students
    WHERE marks > ?
    """;

questions.q: What are Optional best practices?
questions.a: Return Optional from methods that may have no result; use map/flatMap/orElse/orElseGet/ifPresent; never call get() without a check; do not use Optional for fields, parameters or collections.
questions.explain: Optional is a return-type tool that makes absence explicit in the API. An empty Optional is not null, and Optional.of(null) throws.
questions.example: find(id).map(User::name).orElse("unknown")
questions.followUp: orElse vs orElseGet?
questions.tip: orElseGet avoids building a default that is not needed.
questions.code: String name = find(id).map(User::name).orElse("unknown");

questions.q: map vs flatMap?
questions.a: map transforms one element into one element; flatMap transforms each element into a stream and flattens the results into one stream.
questions.explain: Use flatMap for nested collections or Optional chains, such as a list of orders each with many items.
questions.example: orders.stream().flatMap(o -> o.items().stream()).count()
questions.followUp: How do you flatten a List<List<Integer>>?
questions.tip: Say 'map one-to-one, flatMap one-to-many'.

questions.q: collect vs reduce?
questions.a: reduce combines elements into a single value with a binary operator; collect gathers into a container using a Collector, which supports mutable accumulation, grouping and downstream collectors.
questions.explain: Prefer collect for strings and collections, reduce for numeric aggregation. A reduce function must be associative for parallel streams.
questions.example: sum() is a specialised reduce; Collectors.joining() builds a string.
questions.followUp: Why must reduce be associative?
questions.tip: Mention that String concatenation in reduce is O(n^2).
questions.code:
int sum = List.of(1, 2, 3).stream().reduce(0, Integer::sum);
String csv = List.of("a", "b").stream().collect(Collectors.joining(","));

questions.q: How does class loading work?
questions.a: Loading finds the bytecode, linking verifies and prepares it and resolves symbolic references, and initialisation runs static initialisers. Parent-first delegation asks the bootstrap and platform loaders before the application loader.
questions.explain: Class initialisation is lazy and thread-safe, triggered by new, static access or reflection. ClassLoader leaks keep whole applications alive in containers.
questions.example: Class.forName("com.example.Main") triggers loading and initialisation.
questions.followUp: What causes a ClassNotFoundException vs NoClassDefFoundError?
questions.tip: Distinguish missing at lookup vs failed earlier initialisation.
questions.code: Class<?> type = Class.forName("java.lang.String");

questions.q: What does the JIT compiler do?
questions.a: It profiles hot methods and compiles bytecode to native code, applying inlining, escape analysis and loop optimisations. Cold code stays interpreted; deoptimisation rolls back speculative assumptions.
questions.explain: Tiered compilation starts with C1 for fast warm-up and promotes hot code to C2. Microbenchmarks need warm-up and a harness such as JMH.
questions.example: A method called millions of times becomes a prime inlining candidate.
questions.followUp: Why are naive Java microbenchmarks misleading?
questions.tip: Mention warm-up, dead-code elimination and JMH.

questions.q: What are common GC tuning levers?
questions.a: Heap sizing (-Xms/-Xmx), collector choice (G1, ZGC, Shenandoah), pause-time goals (-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis), and young-generation sizing. Start by measuring allocation rate and pause times.
questions.explain: Most throughput problems are allocation problems, not flag problems. Fix object churn first, then tune. Containers need -XX:MaxRAMPercentage rather than fixed sizes.
questions.example: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 -XX:+UseG1GC in a container.
questions.followUp: When would you choose ZGC?
questions.tip: Say 'measure first, tune second'.
questions.code: java -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200 -jar app.jar

questions.q: What is ThreadLocal and when does it leak?
questions.a: ThreadLocal gives each thread its own copy of a value. In pooled threads the value survives between tasks unless remove() is called, which leaks memory and can leak data across users.
questions.explain: Libraries use ThreadLocal for request context, formatters and transactions. Always clear it in a finally block, or use scoped values where available.
questions.example: A DateFormat cached per thread is safe but must be removed in a pool.
questions.followUp: How do virtual threads change ThreadLocal usage?
questions.tip: Mention thread pools plus remove() in finally.

questions.q: synchronized vs ReentrantLock?
questions.a: Both provide mutual exclusion and visibility. ReentrantLock adds tryLock with timeout, interruptible acquisition, fairness and multiple conditions; synchronized is simpler and released automatically.
questions.explain: Prefer synchronized unless you need those advanced features, since manual unlock in finally is easy to get wrong.
questions.example: if (lock.tryLock(1, SECONDS)) { try { ... } finally { lock.unlock(); } }
questions.followUp: What is lock fairness and what does it cost?
questions.tip: Say 'unlock must be in finally'.

questions.q: What is the ForkJoinPool and work stealing?
questions.a: A pool for recursive divide-and-conquer tasks. Idle workers steal subtasks from other workers' deques, keeping all cores busy. Parallel streams use the common pool.
questions.explain: Tasks should avoid blocking I/O, which stalls a worker and can starve the pool. Use managed blockers or a separate executor for blocking work.
questions.example: RecursiveTask<Integer> splitting an array range until a threshold.
questions.followUp: Why is blocking in a parallel stream dangerous?
questions.tip: Mention the common pool is shared JVM-wide.

questions.q: Race condition vs data race?
questions.a: A data race is unsynchronised concurrent access to the same memory with at least one write. A race condition is any timing-dependent correctness bug, which can occur even with proper locking (for example check-then-act).
questions.explain: You can have a race condition without a data race: two synchronized operations composed non-atomically still interleave incorrectly.
questions.example: if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v); is a race condition even on a synchronized map.
questions.followUp: How do you fix check-then-act?
questions.tip: Use computeIfAbsent for atomic check-and-put.
questions.code: map.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(value);

questions.q: What is safe publication?
questions.a: Making a fully constructed object visible to other threads with a happens-before edge: through a volatile field, a static initialiser, a final field, a concurrent collection, or lock handoff.
questions.explain: Without it another thread may see a partially constructed object with default field values, even though the constructor finished in program order.
questions.example: Storing the object in a volatile field or an AtomicReference publishes it safely.
questions.followUp: How do final fields help?
questions.tip: Connect it to the double-checked locking bug.
questions.code:
private volatile Config config;

void reload() { config = new Config(); }

questions.q: How do you write a custom Collector?
questions.a: Implement supplier (new container), accumulator (add one element), combiner (merge two containers for parallel) and finisher (optional final transform).
questions.explain: Collectors.of builds one; most needs are met by teeing, groupingBy with downstream collectors, or collectingAndThen.
questions.example: A collector that joins names into a sorted, comma-separated string.
questions.followUp: Why is the combiner required?
questions.tip: Explain the combiner's role in parallel processing.

questions.q: What are the risks of reflection and serialization?
questions.a: Reflection breaks encapsulation and compile-time checks and can fail under modules or renamed fields. Java serialization bypasses constructors, is fragile across versions and has a history of deserialization vulnerabilities.
questions.explain: Prefer explicit data binding (JSON) or serialization proxies. If you must deserialize untrusted data, use an allow-list filter.
questions.example: serialVersionUID mismatches break compatibility; gadget chains exploit readObject.
questions.followUp: What is a serialization filter?
questions.tip: Mention that records and explicit DTOs are safer than default serialization.

questions.q: What are virtual threads and when do they help?
questions.a: Virtual threads are lightweight threads scheduled by the JVM onto a small pool of carrier threads. They make blocking code scale to many concurrent tasks, especially I/O-bound servers.
questions.explain: They do not speed up CPU-bound work and can pin carrier threads inside synchronized blocks or native calls. Avoid pooling them; create one per task.
questions.example: Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() handles thousands of blocking requests.
questions.followUp: What is pinning?
questions.tip: Say 'great for I/O, not for CPU, do not pool them'.

questions.q: How does pattern matching for switch work?
questions.a: Cases can test types with a binding variable, add guards with when, and destructure records. For sealed hierarchies the compiler enforces exhaustiveness, so no default is needed.
questions.explain: Order matters: more specific patterns must come first. Null must be handled explicitly with case null.
questions.example: case Circle(double r) -> Math.PI * r * r;
questions.followUp: Why is exhaustiveness valuable?
questions.tip: Mention that adding a new permitted subtype becomes a compile error at every switch.

questions.q: How do you find and fix a memory leak in a Java application?
questions.a: Reproduce the growth, capture heap dumps, compare dominator trees, and find objects that should have been collected but are still strongly reachable. Common causes are static caches, listeners never removed, ThreadLocal values and unbounded queues.
questions.explain: Tools: jcmd GC.heap_dump, Eclipse MAT, JFR allocation profiling. Fix by bounding caches, removing listeners, clearing ThreadLocals and closing resources.
questions.example: A static Map<Session, User> that never evicts grows until OutOfMemoryError.
questions.followUp: How do weak references help a cache?
questions.tip: Say 'reachable, not just allocated' — that is the definition of a leak here.
questions.code:
// leak: static map with no eviction
static final Map<String, byte[]> CACHE = new HashMap<>();
